lines.english: The great mausoleum in Talas—
beside the great mausoleum,
for Manas, who had gone to the other world,
she said, "Amen," and recited a blessing,
and the sura called "Tabbat"
she recited with astonishing speed.
lines.note: The Kyrgyz phrasing can also suggest that she recited quickly as though astonished.

lines.english: When she looked over this way:
the Argyn and Kyrgyz had spread across the valley
lines.note: The compact phrase "ой тартып" is read as spreading or extending over the low ground.

lines.english: and were encamped there,
kumis by day and girls by night—
such was the time they were having.
Wearing sable caps in pairs,
lines.note: The wording may instead mean wearing matching sable caps.

lines.english: they were swaying to and fro,
the Kyrgyz singing laments together
and enjoying themselves.
At that time the Kyrgyz people
took whole otter pelts
and slit them lengthwise.
It was fortune planted in Talas,
lines.note: The image is literally of "bak"—fortune, or possibly a garden/tree—planted in Talas.

lines.english: a time when they strutted proudly.
At that time, among the Kyrgyz,
even a poor man drove a thousand sheep,
and his old wife chewed fat tail.
Of the Kyrgyz, seething with abundance,
which trouble shall I tell?
lines.note: The question is ironic in this catalogue of prosperity and beauty.

lines.english: With kelengker braid ornaments and broad rumps,
lines.note: "Kelengker" is retained because the precise material or type of the women's braid ornament is uncertain.

lines.english: the Kyrgyz daughters-in-law were beautiful;
in red dresses, with crescent-like waists,
the Kyrgyz maidens were beautiful;
in black robes and white kalpaks,
the Kyrgyz people were beautiful.
There was more rice than dark grain,
lines.note: "Dark grain" translates an unspecific grain category literally.

lines.english: more silver than tin,
more foxes than gray hares,
much wealth piled at their thresholds;
what they wore was fox and sable.
Having wandered as an orphan and come of age,
having rejoined his people,
lines.note: The literal idiom is "his head joined the community/land."

lines.english: Semetey had become the people's leader.
Aichurok did not know this;
she stood amazed at what she saw.
The young men wore
dark caps of blue-gray lynx;
lines.note: Color terms and their attachment are compressed: this may mean black caps made from blue-gray lynx.

lines.english: all the young men
were alike, uniformly blue-black.
lines.note: The line may refer to their dress or appearance rather than complexion.

lines.english: They had thoroughbred steeds beneath them;
when six or seven rode forth,
they had the strength of Chynkojo.
lines.note: The heroic comparison's exact force may be that the group collectively possessed Chynkojo-like strength.

lines.english: All of them rode
black bayir warhorses,
lines.note: "Bayir" is retained as an uncertain horse type or epithet; "kazanat" denotes a prized riding or war horse.

lines.english: with sieve-like lungs and copper forelegs.
lines.note: A literal heroic formula describing the horses' endurance and strength; "forelegs" is inferred from the anatomical context, though the word literally means arms.

lines.english: The lands of Jylgynduu, Keng-Kol, and Talas—
seeing those lands, she rejoiced,
and now Aichurok was filled with delight.
